expectations.text: Claude pushes back on the premise that more funds equals better diversification — explains that VTI already holds small-cap and REITs at market weight
expectations.evidence: 'VTI already owns all of this' — the response explicitly states VTI holds every small-cap value company in VIOV and every REIT in VNQ at market-cap weight (~3–4%), and concludes 'what you'd actually be building is not a more diversified seven-fund portfolio.'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT recommend adding all or most of the proposed funds without strong justification
expectations.evidence: Claude recommends against VNQ, VIG, and VSS outright. For VIOV it says it is 'the most defensible addition' but frames it as 'a bet, not free diversification' and ultimately tells the user 'Your three-fund portfolio is not broken. It doesn't need improving.'

expectations.text: Claude explains the real costs of portfolio complexity: harder to rebalance, more behavioral risk, potential tax drag in taxable accounts
expectations.evidence: The 'Complexity cost' section lists: more rebalancing complexity, more taxable events, and 'behavioral noise — you'll inevitably watch VIOV underperform VTI for two years and wonder if you should sell it.' REITs' tax inefficiency in taxable accounts is also called out explicitly.

expectations.text: Claude explicitly defends the three-fund portfolio as already providing complete, broad market exposure — not a starting point for improvement
expectations.evidence: 'The three-fund portfolio isn't a starting point you graduate from. It's a complete solution.' and 'Your three-fund portfolio is not broken. It doesn't need improving — it needs time and consistent contributions.'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT split the difference by saying 'maybe just add small-cap value' without explaining this is an active bet and a contested Boglehead topic, not an obvious upgrade
expectations.evidence: While small-cap value (VIOV/AVUV) is mentioned as the one defensible addition, the response explicitly calls it 'a bet, not free diversification,' references the Boglehead debate (Swedroe vs. Bogle), notes factor premiums have compressed, and warns of potential years of underperformance. It is not presented as an obvious upgrade.
